title: ICS 40 cacao (NSIC Cc 01): Characteristics
metaDescription: ICS 40 cacao is a cacao variety from UPLB. See its days to harvest, yield, pest ratings, traits and where it grows best.
excerpt: ICS 40 is a registered cacao variety, also sold or known as NSIC Cc 01. It was registered with the National Seed Industry Council (NSIC) in 2199 as NSIC 1999 Cc 01. UPLB bred it.

heroImage.alt: Young fruit trees planted in straight rows on cleared red soil, the kind of farm where ICS 40 cacao is grown

blocks.text: If you came here looking for NSIC Cc 01, this is the same cacao. The facts below come from the NSIC registry kept by the Bureau of Plant Industry, with notes from its seller and farm sources. Compare it with the others in our [cacao variety finder](/crop-varieties/cacao), or see [every crop variety](/crop-varieties) we list. For the crop itself, read our guide: [Land preparation for tree crops](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation).

blocks.text: When does it bear, and how much?

A registered tree variety is described from its mother tree, not from trial plots. It first bore pods about 17.6 months after planting. A grafted or marcotted tree bears years sooner than one grown from seed, and its yield climbs as the tree grows.

blocks.text: It showed no weak spot in the ratings on record. Still, a resistant variety can break down when a new strain or pest population comes, so keep scouting.

The pests and diseases that hit cacao fields most often: [black pod of cacao](/diseases/cacao-black-pod), [cacao pod borer](/pests/cacao-pod-borer), [mealybug](/pests/mealybug). Our [pest finder](/pests) and [disease finder](/diseases) help you name what you see.
What its seller and farm sources say

items: **Harvest:** First flowers about 18 months, pods about 20 months after planting.
**Fruit:** Green pods turning yellow, about 44 beans per pod, 100 dry beans about 141 g.
Moderately resistant to pod borer, dieback and pod rot.

blocks.text: Why farmers know it: the first cacao on the NSIC list, with many beans per pod (about 44). Check these against what farmers near you have seen, because the same variety can do differently from one town to the next.
Where and when to plant ICS 40 cacao

Plant grafted clones, and mix two or three, because many cacao clones need another clone nearby to set pods. Pick by pod yield and bean size. A registered tree variety is a selection from one proven mother tree, and only grafted, budded or marcotted plants carry its traits. A seedling grown from its seed can turn out quite different. So buy from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, and ask which mother tree the scions came from. Before planting, get the field ready with our guide: [Pagtatanim ng puno](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-puno).

items: Buy grafted or budded plants from an accredited nursery, with the variety name on the tag.
Ask your municipal agriculturist or nearby farmers how it did in your area last season.
Plant a few trees first if the variety is new to your area, before you fill the whole farm.
Write down the planting day, inputs and harvest, so you can compare varieties on your own ground. anee.io keeps these records for you.

items.q: Is NSIC Cc 01 the same as ICS 40?
items.a: Yes. NSIC Cc 01 is another name for ICS 40, registered as NSIC 1999 Cc 01. Seed sellers use both, so ask for either one.

items.q: Where can I buy planting material of ICS 40?
items.a: Buy grafted, budded or marcotted trees from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, so you get the true variety. Ask your provincial agriculture office for the nearest one.
